articleTitle: Fourth IEE Conference on Telecommunications (Conf. Publ. No.371)
GSM roaming-practical experiences
abstract: On the 7 September 1987, mobile network operators within Europe signed a Memorandum Of Understanding, MoU, to produce a mobile telephony system that would be standard across Europe. This became known as GSM-Groupe Speciale Mobile. One ability of the GSM system is to make and receive calls on any other GSM network using the same number. This feature is known as roaming, or in more precise terms: Article 1 of the MoU provides for the establishment of international roaming services whereby a subscriber provided with a service in one country by one of the network operators can also gain access to the service of any other network operator in their respective countries. This is seen as being the main advantage of GSM over the analogue systems. The author explains how roaming works and discusses practical experiences.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The future of optically amplified submarine systems
abstract: The advent of erbium doped fibre amplifiers (EDFA) has revolutionised the options available to submarine cable system planners. It has become possible to extend the range of unrepeatered systems operating at 1.55 mu m to about 300-400 km. The next generation of optical systems, TAT12/13 and TPC5, which are planned for the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans in 1995/6 will use optical amplifiers and operate at 5 Gbit/s per fibre pair. The authors look at constraints on the operation of long haul optically amplified systems and suggest areas where progress needs to be made in order to allow operation at rates beyond 5 Gbit/s. Gordon-Haus jitter and provision of an adequate SNR have been recognised as the limiting factors for soliton systems. However, guiding filters may allow these constraints to be relaxed and higher speed operation achieved. Soliton systems may also offer the promise of multi-channel operation using either two polarisation states or a few WDM channels. The latter requires that the gain of each wavelength channel can be adequately controlled.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An application programming interface for collaborative working
abstract: Experience gained with the implementation of the IBM person-to-person desk top conferencing product, has led to these proposals for an enabling platform which supports an extensive range of collaborative applications. Four interfaces are proposed: (1) an application programming interface (API); (2) a device driver interface; (3) a resources interface; and (4) a data stream. The author discusses the requirements of the API and an architecture for the API is proposed that satisfies these requirements and allows the development of a network based real-time collaborative platform.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Wavelength addressing for an efficient photonic subscriber-loop architecture
abstract: A wavelength-routed photonic subscriber loop architecture, based on the dynamic call-by-call assignment of a single optical carrier to a bidirectional communication rather than to a dedicated LTU/CPE connection is demonstrated. Besides connectivity, the system performs concentration and protection against failures in the central office and is believed to offer a potentially cost effective solution for broadband subscribers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated broadband access
abstract: A generic access scheme, based on ATM techniques, is described that allows one to combine FITL, VHDSL, CATV coaxial lines and radio links in an integrated way. The system is called integrated broadband access, as it provides a common access platform for all services, narrowband and broadband, and as it offers the possibility to combine multiple transmission techniques in a common access architecture. The proposed solution is an extension of the APON presented by Verbiest et al. (see Proceedings 13th International Telecom. Symposium, vol.III, p.49-55, 1992). The main benefits are the bandwidth flexibility, absence of cell loss and inherent policing functionality. The access delays have been evaluated. Possible extensions towards statistical multiplexing gains and concentration have been indicated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multiple access techniques and spectrum utilisation of the GLOBALSTAR mobile satellite system
abstract: The GLOBALSTAR system is a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-based mobile communications system that is interoperable with the current and future public land mobile network. The GLOBALSTAR system concept is based upon technological advancement in two key areas: LEO satellite technology; and cellular telephone technology, including the commercial applications of code division multiple access (CDMA) technologies, progress in time division multiple access technologies. The GLOBALSTAR system uses elements of CDMA technology, combining with satellite multiple beam antenna technology. The following techniques are exploited in obtaining high spectral efficiency and affordable cost per channel, with minimum coordination among different systems: power control in open and closed loops; voice activation; spot beam satellite antenna for frequency reuse; weighted satellite antenna gain; multiple satellite coverage; and satellite changeover. The GLOBALSTAR system design will use the frequency bands 1610-1626.5 MHz for the up-link and 2483.5-2500 MHz for the down-link.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Telecommunications management and mobility
abstract: The author discusses the important role of telecommunications management in supporting and providing mobility in personal communications. Management issues specific to both terminal and personal mobility are identified and discussed. These management issues are subsequently used as the basis for possible approaches to analysing, designing and implementing management systems with the functionality required for networks offering mobility. Examples from Universal Personal Telephony (UPT), the Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS), and from the RACE II MONET project are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Telepresence-visual telecommunications into the next century
abstract: The authors describe a selection of telepresence systems and services that are currently being investigated and developed. Each can be fully realised with present day technology, and most can operate, albeit at a reduced service level, over the existing network. The authors draw attention to their potential and likely importance in future telecommunications. Topics covered include mobile telepresence; video walls; electronic whiteboards; instant facsimile; teleconferencing; hands in the screen interfaces; virtual reality; and 3D presentation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MODAL: an enabling technology for wireless access
abstract: Future mobile radio systems must use ever higher radio frequencies as spectral congestion effectively removes lower frequencies from availability. Future broadband mobile services (e.g. MBS) will use mm-wave frequencies and utilise a microcellular architecture. The limitations of fibre/radio for these applications are outlined and a novel solution, based on optical heterodyning, is proposed. A RACE funded research programme is investigating this approach and the authors describe the demonstrator that will be built. Applications for MODAL (microwave optical duplex antenna link) type systems are discussed and some of the most significant results achieved to date are summarised. The authors outline a novel solution to the problem of providing a connection between a base station and a remote antenna for a mobile access system operating at mm-wave frequencies. Optical technology has been adopted to remove the need for mm-wave signal sources whilst optical fibre is used to interconnect the base station and the antenna thereby ensuring both low installation and maintenance costs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A distributed rural telephone system for developing countries
abstract: The authors describe work on a novel rural radio telephony system which, by using an exchangeless network structure, is uniquely suited to providing a basic telephone service to widely-separated sites, for example villages in developing countries where telephone provision is rare. They lay out the traffic analysis of a distributed telephone system which is designed to meet these requirements at a realistic level of equipment cost.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: LAN and switching systems: flexibility and performance through architectural design
abstract: Faced with the explosion of new services and user demand, telecommunication systems must remain open, flexible, and capable of absorbing new components. To meet this challenge both in terms of modularity and performance as well as upgradeability and security, one approach is to structure a system composed of multiple processor stations connected to a local network. The authors describe how the structure of a telecommunications system can be modelled by loosely distributing its application software onto an adaptable number of physical machines interconnected by a highly secured communication medium based on LAN technology. The main characteristics of such a structure are also discussed and include traffic adaptability, functional evolution, and fault tolerance. Issues related to local network standards, the increasingly widespread use of integrating components, and the possibility of integrating constantly evolving technology are presented. The authors emphasize a number of specific implementation options, and address innovative solutions mainly related to system extensions and defense.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimum structures of space switching fabrics for SDH cross-connect equipment
abstract: A number of telecommunications operating companies have identified a need for compact SDH cross-connect equipment and multiplexers with cross-connect capabilities for deployment in all three tiers of a manageable digital communications network. The way in which the space switching components of the switching fabric are built and the way in which the functionality is distributed amongst IC packages and circuit cards determine the density of the switching fabric and the physical size of the control memory. These characteristics of single stage cross-point and multi-stage Clos networks are investigated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SDH rings for distributed cross-connect functionality
abstract: SDH (synchronous digital hierarchy) based systems represent a major advance over current PDH (plesiochronous digital hierarchy) based transmission systems. The authors examine the role SDH rings play in SDH transmission systems, in particular the benefits obtained from the autonomous protection switching (APS) and distributed bandwidth management (DBM) features. An SDH ring deployment strategy is described showing how SDH rings can be used in conjunction with cross-connects to build high speed transmission networks that are flexible, survivable and cost effective.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Managed transport networks-the international dimension
abstract: Evolving technologies, user needs and regulatory environments are providing opportunities to develop transport networks on an international basis. The author discusses the architectural and design issues associated with evolving transport networks and describes examples of transport networks being planned and in operation (GEN, METRAN and GNP).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The applicability of LEO satellites to 3rd generation networks
abstract: The prime objective of third generation mobile systems is to achieve a fully integrated digital mobile satellite/terrestrial communications network, capable of supporting voice and data communications throughout the world in either a satellite, cellular or cordless environment. The authors highlight some of the issues that need to be taken into account when considering integrating a LEO system with a terrestrial network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new multiplexor for B-ISDN connectionless data traffic
abstract: The authors present a new idea for multiplexing cell streams of data traffic which, by using a protocol to mark only some of the cells as discardable, reduces the number of messages corrupted and maintains the quality of service. A description is given of the function and uses of the cell loss priority (CLP) bit, with particular reference made to its use for marking which cells are potentially discardable within the multiplexor. A detailed description is given of the protocol proposed for controlling cell discards. Then some simulation experiments are described, based on a transputer array which is being used to assess the performance of the protocol. Finally the conclusions and areas of further study are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ATM network dimensioning: an overview
abstract: The paper is based on work undertaken by the network planning task group (TGV) of CEC RACE project R1022 in addressing the topic of ATM dimensioning from the viewpoint of a network planner (rather than a teletraffic theorist). It summarises traffic work undertaken within R1022 by presenting the important issues related to ATM traffic engineering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of smart cards in personal communication systems security
abstract: The authors discuss the application of IC cards (or 'smart cards') in the security of personal communication systems. The architecture of smart cards is examined, as are their functional capabilities. An overview of the security requirements of personal communication systems applicable to smart cards is presented. Methods of implementing typical smart card security schemes are proposed, together with practical examples and rationale. The significant operational and security advantages achievable by the use of smart cards in security systems are discussed. The authors conclude with details of current limitations of smart card solutions to the security of personal communication systems, and details of likely future developments in smart card functionality.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An approach to resolving feature interaction in advanced intelligent network services
abstract: The authors examines aspects of feature interaction in relation to the development of IN applications within the framework of the Bellcore AIN (release 1) and the emerging CCITT/ETSI Capability Set 1 architectures. Current provisions only allow a single point of control for IN features. This is inadequate as it does not permit services to be distributed between service control points and limits the ability of network providers to acquire features from different sources. The author proposes simple negotiation technique for the control of call processing events which can be used to resolve a whole class of feature interactions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The integration of ATM, SDH and PON technology in the access network
abstract: ATM has been presented as the new network paradigm that will integrate all present day and future broadband services. The author attempts to show that in fact it is the managed transmission network which is the new paradigm and that this has been implemented in SDH as well as ATM and can be extended into PON systems. The author also attempts to show that ATM is unsuited to current narrowband and wideband services, but that a PON based access system can be optimised for current services while still capable of providing ATM services on an evolutionary basis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Coherent optic switching: applications and architectures
abstract: The authors list and detail several applications requiring a single stage, non-blocking, broadband, switching capability. They describe several switches, which are variants of one basic coherent optics switch architecture, to meet the requirements of those applications. The architectures will enable multiplexed carriers to be switched with minimal transit delay or distortion. The passive optic interconnect is used not only to carry the channels to be switched, but also all the necessary switch control and frequency stabilisation control information. Consequently because the optical budget also permits some of the optic combiners and splitters to be distributed, very distributed switch arrangements are possible. For the applications listed, the authors show the suitability of wavelength division optics for the control distribution and coherent optics for the switching functions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An environment for rapid service development (intelligent networks)
abstract: The author considers the problem of rapid IN service development, taking the whole development lifecycle into consideration, from initial service invention to final network deployment of a validated service. Service development is considered as consisting of four major stages: service invention, service definition, service production, and service integration. Each of these stages is discussed together with an integrated rapid service development environment developed by GPT. It has a comprehensive set of tools which assist the service developer at each stage of the service development process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical cable systems for the local loop
abstract: The authors show a number of the considerations being actively pursued to develop optimal solutions for the installation of a future proof optical access network infrastructure. New developments are continually improving the economics of this introduction and altering perceptions of the best evolutionary approach. In the long term the authors believe that fibre will be ubiquitous with increasing penetration of direct fibre customer links. Topics discussed include network architectures; cable design; interconnection and installation; and system reliability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integration of new telecommunications services into computer networks
abstract: New, high performance, telecommunications services are emerging for the transport of data. Frame relay, which originated in CCITT, has been used for some years in constructing private data networks while, more recently, public frame relay services have been introduced. Switched multi-megabit data service (SMDS) has been defined by Bellcore in the US as a public, packet switching service with corresponding specifications now being developed for Europe. Experience has been gained in numerous trials and public services are already available in the US with European services being planned. These data networking services are briefly introduced. Their distinguishing characteristics are described primarily from the perspective of the customer premises equipment (CPE) that connect to the networks. Approaches are discussed for the integration of these new services into common computer network protocols.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Service addressing: an approach to the problems of heterogeneity and distribution for VISION O.N.E
abstract: It is a self-evident truth that most telecommunications systems are large and complex; they are now increasingly both distributed and heterogeneous. It is now apparent that the software components which comprise them would benefit by being parcelled into discrete units exhibiting well-specified interfaces, offering a service to the rest of the system. Service addressing is a mechanism which is intended to support a system architecture based on service requests and service provision. VISION O.N.E. is a strategy established by GPT and Siemens for the evolution of telecommunications. It comprises all the innovative network elements required for the high-performance networks of the future, building on a set of product platforms. It is an example of a distributed and heterogeneous system. There are two key issues: how the system software is structured and when, and how it operates during run time. The proposed scheme relies on many of the concepts from the domain of object-orientation and the ANSA (advanced network systems architecture) project. The author discusses the role of service addressing in VISION O.N.E.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Introducing ATM for the business and residential customer
abstract: Before the final BISDN will be available to everybody, some decades will pass. It is therefore important that introduction strategies with a clear evolutionary path to the future are worked out. Two introduction strategies are described here, along with their early application. The first is mainly intended for business customers and offers in an initial phase ATM crossconnect functionality. The second is preferentially for residential users and offers initially POTS/NISDN and analog TV services. Both solutions can easily be upgraded step by step to a full ATM based BISDN.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical amplifiers extend the range of repeaterless submarine systems
abstract: Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFA) have seen rapid developments in the past few years, and they fit especially well the needs of repeaterless submarine links. For these links, the demand is very strong for ever longer spans, in the range of 150 km to 350 km. The applications are in continent-island, island-island, or coastal 'festooned' links. Aside from using low-loss silica-core fiber and error-correcting codes, optical amplifiers offer a practical way to increase the power budget of repeaterless links. First, an EDFA can be used to increase the transmitter output power. At the receiver end, an EDFA can be used as a preamplifier, either at the receiver site or at some distance with remote pumping from the receiver terminal, in order to obtain a better gain/noise compromise. With erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, commercial repeaterless systems up to 300 km at 622 Mbit/s or 260 km at 2.5 Gbit/s can be implemented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power budgets for long-haul optically amplified systems
abstract: Power budgets are used in the system planning of all submarine and terrestrial optical systems. They enable system owners and suppliers to identify the margin that exists in the system design and to compare this with the specified performance objectives. The author considers how a power budget can be developed for an optically amplified system. Two possible starting points for these are computer system simulations or a simple model of amplifier noise concatenation; the benefits and drawbacks of each are considered. Both give a measure of the expected performance for an idealised system, that is there are a number of effects that are not taken into account. The power budget is used to subtract from this idealised system performance these additional impairments to give the actual expected performance. These additional impairments are identified and considered individually.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A business user's overview
abstract: Medium-to-large businesses tend to be polarised in their views towards telecommunications: those with limited vision regard the provision of telecommunications as a necessary evil, the costs of which must be managed downwards as part of a disciplined approach to overheads; while those who have not been put off by the technology or the jargon recognise telecommunications as one of the great enablers of our times, and seek actively to bend the offerings of the telecommunications suppliers to the benefit of their own bottom line. The author discusses this latter business user's view. The author sets the view within the framework of UK regulation and competition, and also the European aspect.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SDH add/drop multiplexer rings in Northern Ireland
abstract: BT Northern Ireland has introduced a network of optical fibre rings into the province as part of an EEC-assisted project known as STAR (Special Telecommunications Action for Regional Development). This network consists of three fibre rings, each equipped with STM-1 add/drop multiplexers and it represents one of the first applications of SDH rings anywhere in the world. The authors describe the SDH equipment used in the Northern Ireland STAR (NISTAR) project and discuss the protection and synchronisation strategies employed in the network. This is followed by an outline of the new testing and commissioning techniques that are required to characterise this equipment and to establish an operational ring network. Finally results of initial network performance tests are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Second-generation erbium-doped fibre amplifiers for advanced optical communications
abstract: The erbium-doped fibre amplifier (EDFA) has seen rapid development and is now established as a key component in future optical networks. The authors modify and optimise the amplifier characteristics for a given application. They discuss the performance of a composite EDFA with an integral isolator. It is shown that this configuration exhibits high gains and quantum-limited noise figure (NF) at relatively low pump powers. A novel configuration of an optical limiting amplifier is presented which exhibits a input-signal dynamic range in excess of 30 dB. An optical equalising amplifier is demonstrated which is based on an erbium-doped twin-core fibre. This fibre geometry shows wavelength-dependent spatial (longitudinal) hole burning, thus, increasing the effective inhomogeneous broadening in the amplifier and provides enhanced output-signal equalisation in a multichannel system. Finally, the potential of the EDFA as a compact source of high-peak power and high-energy pulses, for medical and military applications, is also explored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New technology opportunities in cellular radio
abstract: A major opportunity now faces the cellular radio industry; that is the possibility to address the mass consumer market, providing mobile communications for everyone at an affordable price. The author shows how new technology, particularly in the area of radio and base-station systems will be an enabling factor in addressing the new market by reducing costs and by facilitating the development of higher capacity networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: International ISDN: the new digital infrastructure
abstract: The main issues covered include the following: Euro-ISDN; user requirements; the changing economic climate; closer cooperation with manufacturers, suppliers and telecommunication operators; and how are users making a difference.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Virtual private networks in Europe: growth, standardisation and evolution
abstract: Virtual private network (VPN) services offered by telecommunications companies (telcos) are being exploited by many large multinational businesses in order to reap the benefits of pricing economies, financial accountability, network rationalisation and the management control that outsourcing of telecomms can provide. Bilateral agreements between European telcos to offer international VPN services are an enabler for increased service transparency between disparate national VPNs. Resulting standardisation of aspects of the national services is likely to impact the development of common control signalling (CCS) systems, feature sets and service management capabilities. Intelligent network (IN) platforms will offer the opportunity for enhanced VPN services by interconnection at the intelligent level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Frequency sharing between LEO systems
abstract: The coordination process between LEO satellite systems is examined for both forward and return links, and for different examples of access schemes. It is shown that the mobile to satellite link would suffer a minimum loss of capacity provided that techniques such as power control, frequency planning, and/or polarisation isolation, are implemented. On the other hand, the satellite to mobile link encounters more difficulties since the return link received a secondary status in the same frequency bandwidth. In this case, coordination would only be achieved with satellite antennas showing isolation levels higher than 40 dB for the sidelobes and higher than 60 dB for the backlobes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New networks for eastern Germany
abstract: The important task of establishing networks in eastern Germany offers Deutsche Telekom a unique chance to apply the latest technologies. This helps to provide the eastern part of Germany with telecom services that are in line with customers' demands. At the same time a genuinely future-oriented infrastructure can be implemented. The western part of Germany will also benefit from the introduction of new technical systems on a larger scale, because higher volumes should lead to more economical conditions for the procurement of these new technical systems. Topics discussed include SDH network components, fibre-in-the-loop systems and wireless local loop.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An approach to location registration and mobility management for dynamic satellite constellations
abstract: Low/medium Earth orbit satellite constellations are expected to play a key role in any future global mobile communications system. Mobility management is examined for these constellations. When an advanced terrestrial type of approach is taken in examining user mobility, a location instability (or flip-flop) is found to occur. It is seen to result in a large signalling overhead. Two new approaches, both based on a similar idea, are proposed which significantly reduce the signalling overhead for such constellations. Rather than associating a mobile terminal with an exact location, the new approach is to associate it, through a single Earth station, which may or may not have an associated team of Earth stations, with what may loosely be described as a location area. Through this association the network can contact the terminal if required to do so. A slight average increase in call set-up time is the cost of the reduction in system signalling. The use of this new protocol for network mobility management results in an important increase in network efficiency for certain constellation types.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fairness and optimality in ATM communication networks
abstract: The author presents a method of analysing a queueing system that features an arbitrary number of priority levels. This model is used to study the effect of prioritising a proportion of broadband traffic in a simple model of a network. The results indicate that, given the assumptions outlined in the results section, the network busy hour utilisation could be increased by 13%.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Personal communications service in fixed and mobile networks
abstract: After discussing the definition of personal communications services, the author considers the following topics: personal service environment; intelligent network implementation of personal communications service; service development for personal communications; personal communications service in mobile networks; ease of use for fixed network PCS/UPT; access to home network features; and service management and billing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Mobile telematics-creating a demand for mobile data
abstract: The author first contrasts the growth in demand for mobile data with that for cellular telephony. It is suggested that the key factor that will stimulate the growth in mobile data is the supply of attractive total solutions for real business needs. The author then focuses on the specific set of applications collectively called road transport informatics. The services and facilities these applications may require are identified in the context of the possible transfer modes for mobile data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Personal communications-service concepts and functionality evolution
abstract: Personal communications systems provide flexibility to telecommunications subscribers by offering both terminal and personal mobility. Terminal mobility can be achieved by a lightweight cordless terminal that a subscriber can carry everywhere. The personal mobility allows subscribers ubiquitous access to all subscribed services, and flexible billing for various types of usage (e.g., business, personal). Personal mobility is currently available for outgoing calls with various telephone calling cards. For incoming calls, several telephone companies are offering call forwarding feature. A new concept of assigning a personal telecommunication number (PTN) to a subscriber that can be resident in a database of the intelligent network (IN), is being considered by service providers globally. The PTN will facilitate access to subscribed services and the location of the subscriber. The Universal Personal Telecommunications (UPT) is a PTN based service which is similar to Freephone except for charging aspects, in that, the caller may pay for all or part of the call.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Emerging intelligent network services: a corridor to personal communications
abstract: The coming era of personal communications networks (PCN) will build on IN technology. The PCN's wireless access and mobility capabilities will spur services that will profoundly affect everyday life, and enhance telephone company revenues. Because of similarities between IN and PCN, many of the fundamental technological hurdles have already been anticipated. The authors look at the personal communications. They then discuss the target architecture for personal communications. Finally, they present the potential services and products that will appear in this high-growth market.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Artificial intelligence for resource management in telecommunications
abstract: The authors highlight the reasons why AI is an appropriate solution to telecommunications problems and present several AI techniques and their applications. They also highlight the area of resource management and present the work being carried out at Strathclyde University, in this field. The system developed for resource allocation problems has three driving forces: a stochastic nature, a distributed architecture and some local improvement facilities, and offers some promising results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Introducing transparencies by modelling intelligent network data
abstract: The intelligent network architecture is aimed at introducing flexibility in service provisioning. A particular aspect of flexibility is described as the transparency requirement. It refers to the capability of service to be designed independently of the underlying network configuration. Obviously, production methodology and tools are required to meet such a challenge. The author describes an external data model which allows the IN service designer to: comprehensively describe data; write programs independently of data distribution; migrate data or programs separately; and respect performance constraints. The gains of such an approach are to: provide requested transparencies; increase the flexibility of the intelligent network architecture; allow for migration activities; alleviate maintenance by increasing the service creation capabilities and by improving documentation; and ease the tuning of services and performances.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Outsourcing-telecommunication services
abstract: Within a review of telecommunications, it will be necessary to consider the benefits of using facilities management (FM) and outsourcing. This can be a partial or total solution to a company's telecommunications service requirements. A common form of FM is the systems and services maintenance contracts. Equally, outsourcing should now be well understood, for computer software and services companies have been in this market for over 20 years. The author discusses various aspects of outsourcing and gives examples as follows: the use of external experts, WAN, PABX and LAN (Ethernet). The author proposes that outsourcing can provide a solution to all telecommunications activities; with the exception of the business strategy, the definition of deliverables and the management of the end-users expectations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Some multimedia traffic characterisation and measurement results
abstract: The authors discuss traffic characterisation and measurements made of experimental multimedia (including audio and video) traffic on the CAR and PREPARE experimental networks, and the IP pilot service on the UK JANET network. They describe the PREPARE experimental architecture and the proposed SuperJANET architecture. They summarise the characteristics of the various media and some of the architectural issues concerning multimedia conferencing. They present detailed results for measurements of shared files, shared windows, audio and video on the current JANET II network. Finally, they draw some conclusions about the future of multimedia services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Telecommunications Information Networking Architecture
abstract: While voice traffic still dominates in telecommunication networks, there is a steady increase in the traffic of other types of information. The adoption of ATM and SDH in broadband networks will provide a flexible and service-independent standard for switching and transport infrastructure that is capable of supporting all information transfer requirements. To exploit this flexibility, the software architecture of telecommunication services and systems must be equally flexible. The Telecommunications Information Networking Architecture (TINA) is an architecture based on state-of-the-art distributed processing and service delivery technologies that will enable the efficient introduction, delivery, management and maintenance of telecommunications services and systems. The specification of this architecture is the principle objective of the recently established TINA Research Consortium. The authors present an overview of the technical activities of this Consortium.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The evolution of connectionless service support in B-ISDN
abstract: The network evolution strategy for connectionless service support in B-ISDN is described. First, an overview is given of how today's MAN networks provide connectionless service. Subsequently the evolution of connectionless service support in an ATM based B-ISDN is highlighted. The various methods of LAN interconnection via ATM networks and finally the introduction and operation of connectionless servers in the B-ISDN are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New multimedia services based on the hypermedia paradigm
abstract: The author analyzes the impact of the hypermedia notion on multimedia integration evolution, introducing a new information unit called hypermedia composition, and outlining several hypermedia based services. Some guidelines needed for the object oriented design of a hypermedia kernel are presented. Within the R1038 RACE project, a multimedia terminal has been developed which provides hypermedia services and is a suitable platform for the future research in this area. The main characteristics of this terminal and the terminal adapter developed are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Supervisory options for fibre optical amplifier systems
abstract: Optical transmission systems using optical amplifiers as repeaters will require remote monitoring and control as part of the network management of the system. Methods used on regenerative systems, which utilise access to the data signal at each repeater, are inappropriate for optically amplified systems. With optical amplifiers, two categories of supervisory have been identified; passive and active. For long or medium haul systems, either submarine or landline, the passive approach offers simplicity but no detailed information on the amplifier status. On the other hand, an active supervisory offers the possibility of a very detailed profile of the amplifier status, but at the expense of complexity. In general, the optimum supervisory system depends on the details of the application, the capabilities of the technology and the reliability requirements. However, in short to medium haul applications passive systems may be optimum because of their simplicity. The authors introduce the options available for optical amplifier supervisory, including system design, and give details of one option that has been successfully demonstrated over medium and long haul amplifier systems. This option is the integrated optical supervisory system using gain modulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic performance assessment of speech recognisers through telephone quality speech databases
abstract: Performance assessment of speech recognisers is one of the major area of interest in the field of speech processing technology. The reasons for such an interest stem from the intrinsic difficulty of the task in terms of repeatability, reliability and validity of the results. It is in fact meaningless to declare any performance measurement without specifying the boundary conditions in which those results were achieved. This consideration becomes even more crucial when the telephone environment is concerned. The authors cover two separate aspects: the generation of telephone grade speech corpora and the assessment of a speech recogniser with both clean and telephone grade speech corpus, the latter being derived from the clean speech version. For the first aspect, the authors describe a complete procedure to generate telephone grade speech corpora; it could be used either to generate completely new corpora or to degrade a given clean corpus to its telephone grade equivalent. Concerning the second aspect, the authors focus on a European standard multilingual corpus, the EUROM 0 CD ROM that has been used twice for a comparative assessment with the same speech recogniser.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The global office
abstract: The author examines the global office, its structure, how people will work in it, the work they will do and the demands they will place on communications technology. A number of contrasting work scenarios are described and analysed to determine the telecommunications and computing facilities needed to meet their requirements. Many of the facilities are available, but what is lacking is their integration into a coherent system that presents a uniform user interface for both data communications and data processing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multimedia advanced CDMA systems
abstract: Third generation high capacity CDMA mobile systems will be able to provide multimedia services. A particular spreading method that supports a flexible multirate radio interface is reported. This is based on low rate orthogonal convolutional (LOROC) codes. A simulation model has been built to verify arguments. The outcomes of the simulations clearly show the capability of this approach to provide low crosscorrelation interference among multirate users. A nonregenerative multiple access interference cancellation method that does not require knowledge or tracking of other user signals and can be applied to both the BS and the MS is then presented. It can be combined perfectly with the LOROC codec and provide interference cancellation irrespectively of the various transmission rates.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Telecommunications in Sierra Leone; from Strowger to fully digital switching
abstract: The author gives an overview of the development process of the communications industry in Sierra Leone, a developing country in West Africa, against the background of the quality of its infrastructures, its educational base (academic and vocational) and of course its economy. The roles of the national telecommunications company (SLNTC) and the national external telecommunications company (SLET) are discussed and their directions in the light of their plan of action are catalogued. These two companies with a strong government partnership enjoy a monopoly in internal and external communications respectively, although there are growing indications of a change in this scenario.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Impact of the mobile GSM-F, digital radio and satellite technologies in rural communications for the next generations
abstract: In order to forecast the most convenient technology for the rural communications market, the author presents a comparative analysis among mobile GSM-F (GSM), digital multiple access radio point-to-multipoint (PMP) and satellite Globalstar (STAR) technologies with an application example, and their impact for three scenarios; years 1992/93, 1996/97 and 2000. In the rural areas with low grouping factor, the trend for the use of GSM and Globalstar technologies is growing and the trend for the use of PMP technology is decreasing. The PMP technology will continue to offer economical services within rural areas that have a moderate grouping factor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An automated system for frequency planning of cellular radio networks
abstract: The automated frequency planning system is based on the availability of a reliable prediction tool. In this case, the Vodafone PACE system is used. Coverage predictions for every cell in the network are held in a database. In the Vodafone TACS network, this database contains predictions for each 250 m square in the UK, and totals nearly 1 GByte. The task of frequency planning may be split into four stages. These are described in turn and consist of interference analysis, exclusion matrix generation, frequency allocation, and checking the plan.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A design for multimedia desk-to-desk conferencing
abstract: The authors describe an interactive multimedia application for cooperative work known as desk-to-desk conferencing. The application enables participants to communicate with others sharing personal computer screens in real time and work together on common images. It is targeted for the broad set of connected personal computers and requires little effort to install and use. The authors review the requirements and benefits expected from such applications and the technologies that make them possible today. They describe their experience at IBM in developing a desk-to-desk conferencing system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The LANC-bringing local ATM to the workstation
abstract: The authors describe Lancaster University's experimental networked multimedia workstation. This workstation retains many of the ideas of the original multimedia network interface system and includes new features to enhance the performance of the workstation and communications. The authors consider that taking ATM to the devices places too great an overhead on the devices where a much simpler and more suitable interface can be used. ATM is too large for device interconnection in a workstation, but 32 bit mini-cells are an ideal size. The LANC is a simple switch which uses such mini cells for connecting a small number of devices and provides the devices with a simple interface which can perform data transfer with characteristics suited for multimedia. The ability to multicast to a number of devices on the LANC is implemented in a very simple and efficient way.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multimedia communication
abstract: Based on the RACE project MCPR (Multimedia Communication Processing and Representation) Alcatel SEL has realized a multimedia terminal system to be connected to Alcatel's broadband ATM (asynchronous transfer mode) switch with a user access rate of 150 Mbit/s. The multimedia terminal adaptor approach was chosen to enable the MCPR system to be connected also to various experimental ATM environments. This working platform is used for evaluation and stepwise refinement of user and network relevant functionalities. The authors discuss the architectural implementation and communication aspects relevant to terminal design and describe the configuration and experience of a demonstration given during Telecom '91 at the Geneva fair.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Resource management in multimedia communication stacks
abstract: The authors present a set of key quality of service (QOS) requirements and map these requirements onto a provisional QOS architecture (QOS-A) which has emerged from an experimental system designed and implemented at Lancaster. Because of the likely complexity of a fully general QOS-A, the scope of the discussion is limited to aspects of a QOS-A for the support of continuous media communications. The authors also concentrate on ATM at the network layer rather than considering the full range of multiservice networks. However, a generalised QOS-A should eventually be extensible to incorporate other areas of QOS provision such as real-time control systems, file transfer and real-time transaction processing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Will B-ISDN services meet the needs of distributed multimedia communications?
abstract: The author discusses the harmonization of B-ISDN, the OSI Reference Model and the emerging multimedia end user service requirements. The key communication requirements of distributed multimedia computing are presented. A short summary of advances in the specification of the B-ISDN/AAL (ATM adaptation layer) services and protocols is used as the basis for mapping of the requirements to the AAL services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
